name: Things you should definitely ghost
what: Creators dress as ghosts holding signboards that list common mistakes or bad habits in their industry, ending with a better solution.
format: Skit with signboards in ghost costume
why_now: It is the peak of Halloween season and combines seasonal fun with educational authority.
brand_use: A finance client could have a 'ghost' list outdated saving habits to avoid, while a tech client could list 'ghosting' old software for their new platform. It’s a low-cost way to show personality while providing value.
example_brief: A banking brand uses a ghost to list 'hidden fees' and 'manual transfers' as things to ghost in favor of their app.

name: Getting robbed
what: A single-shot comedy skit where the creator is so distracted by their phone that they don't notice someone stealing their bag in the background.
why_now: It is a high-engagement humor format that peaked in mid-October.
brand_use: An entertainment or news client can use this to show how 'addictive' or 'engaging' their content is. The text overlay would say 'Me when [Brand Name] drops a new episode/article.'
example_brief: A streaming service shows a viewer losing their bag because they are too focused on a season finale.
risk: Ensure the 'theft' is clearly comedic and staged to avoid alarming viewers.

name: Ramalama Costume Walk
what: A low-angle reveal where the camera focuses on feet walking toward it before cutting to a full Halloween costume reveal.
why_now: Halloween costume reveals are the dominant content type this week.
brand_use: Perfect for retail or fashion clients to showcase seasonal collections or for an agency to show off the team's office Halloween costumes in a high-energy way.
example_brief: A fashion retailer uses the low-angle walk to reveal four different 'last-minute' costume ideas using their current stock.

name: The 'Oh look' trend
what: A duo reacts with dramatic panic to a stressful scenario before instantly switching to calm when a simple solution is presented.
why_now: It is a highly effective 'problem/solution' framework currently circulating.
brand_use: Ideal for B2B or service-based clients. Show the 'panic' of a complex task (like tax or logistics) and the 'calm' of using the client's service.
example_brief: A logistics brand shows a business owner panicking over a lost shipment, then instantly calm when they open the brand's tracking app.

name: Two Fishes (Unpopular Opinions)
what: Lip-syncing Love Island audio to defend a questionable or illogical opinion with total confidence.
sound: Corbin Mims / CorbinGPT Love Island USA audio
why_now: The audio is trending for its 'confidently wrong' energy which drives high comment section engagement.
brand_use: Brands can use this to defend a harmless but 'controversial' brand take, like 'Pineapple belongs on pizza' or 'Socks with sandals is a vibe.'
example_brief: A food brand uses the audio to defend a weird but delicious snack combination.
risk: Avoid actually controversial or political topics; keep it light and product-related.

name: Text message from -A
what: A text-on-screen hook referencing Pretty Little Liars that 'exposes' a secret habit or clever shortcut, signed '-A'.
sound: pll purposes only ty - demi devito
why_now: Nostalgia-driven trends are peaking, and the format is perfect for 'relatable' brand confessions.
brand_use: A brand can 'expose' a secret way customers use their product. For example, a skincare brand showing someone using their moisturizer on their elbows.
example_brief: A coffee brand posts: 'I saw you buying a second latte before 10am. -A'.

name: Netflix Documentary Chair-Sit
what: Creators sit in a chair with dramatic lighting and music, narrating a mundane subject with the gravity of a true-crime documentary.
why_now: The 'dramatic irony' of treating small things with high production value is a growing aesthetic trend.
brand_use: An agency could use this to 'investigate' the mystery of who keeps stealing oat milk from the office fridge, or a brand could narrate the 'history' of their best-selling product.
example_brief: A snack brand narrates the 'harrowing journey' of a chip from the bag to the bowl.

name: Fan Transition
what: Creators lie on the floor and use a ceiling fan (or fan-blade overlay) to transition between different outfits or looks.
why_now: It is the leading high-production-value transition trend for October.
brand_use: Perfect for fashion or beauty clients to show a 'week of looks' or a 'day-to-night' transformation. It feels premium and polished.
example_brief: A department store uses the fan transition to show four different Halloween party outfits.
risk: Requires slightly more editing skill to time the 'blade' pass with the outfit change.

name: Daily GRWM Loading
what: A 'Get Ready With Me' video that uses a loading bar (0% to 100%) to show the progression from pajamas to a finished look.
why_now: The 'loading' visual is a strong hook that increases watch time as viewers wait for 100%.
brand_use: Great for any 'transformation'—a home decor brand showing a room makeover, or a makeup brand showing a 5-minute face.
example_brief: A skincare brand shows a 'Morning Glow Loading' bar that hits 100% after using their serum.

name: October is all about me
what: Using Drake's 'October is all about me' audio to showcase 'main character energy' or a brand's dominance this month.
why_now: It is the definitive 'mid-October' anthem for creators and brands alike.
brand_use: A brand can use this to highlight a 'Product of the Month' or a major October launch, positioning the product as the star of the season.
example_brief: A beverage brand shows their seasonal spiced latte with the text 'October is all about me'.

name: Gen Z Marketing Trend
what: A meta-trend where brands parody 'Gen Z marketing' by using excessive slang, emojis, and chaotic edits.
why_now: Self-aware corporate humor is currently the most effective way for brands to build 'cool' capital.
brand_use: The agency can create a video for a client where an 'older' executive tries to use Gen Z slang to sell a very traditional product.
example_brief: An insurance company uses 'no cap' and 'skibidi' to explain their latest policy in a satirical way.
risk: Can feel 'cringe' if not executed with clear satirical intent.

name: My Reaction (Ranking)
what: Creators rank items or give opinions on niche topics using only facial expressions and a specific audio track.
why_now: It’s a low-friction way to participate in niche community debates.
brand_use: A travel client could rank 'Types of travelers' or a food client could rank 'Pizza toppings' using just the creator's face to show approval or disgust.
example_brief: A tech brand ranks 'Office habits' from 'Elite' to 'Straight to Jail' using facial reactions.

name: October Aesthetics (Cozy/Nostalgic)
what: Slow, cinematic montages of autumn moments: coffee pours, falling leaves, and cozy interiors.
sound: we fell in love in october - girl in red
why_now: The 'Autumnal' vibe is at its peak before the pivot to Christmas content in November.
brand_use: Perfect for lifestyle, home, or F&B brands to 'romanticize' their products in a seasonal context.
example_brief: A candle brand shows a slow-motion match strike and flame flicker in a dimly lit, cozy room.
risk: Can feel generic if there isn't a unique brand angle or high-quality cinematography.

name: Suspect Trend
what: Creators jog in slow motion while a friend 'calls out' a funny, hyper-specific description of them as if they are a police suspect.
why_now: It is a popular 'team-bonding' format that shows off company culture.
brand_use: The agency can use this to introduce team members. 'Suspect is 5'11, drinks 6 coffees a day, and still uses Comic Sans.'
example_brief: A creative team introduces their lead designer as a 'suspect' who 'refuses to use any color other than beige'.

name: Money can’t buy happiness, but...
what: Creators use the prompt 'Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy [Product/Experience]' to show how their offering boosts mood.
why_now: It is a classic, high-conversion retail format that has resurfaced this week.
brand_use: Direct-to-camera product placement. 'Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy this 7-step skincare routine.'
example_brief: A pet brand shows a happy dog with the text: 'Money can't buy happiness, but it can buy a subscription box for this guy.'
risk: Can feel overly 'salesy' if the product isn't genuinely delightful.

name: Goo Goo Muck (Halloween Movement)
what: Creators move a person or a Halloween prop in sync with the beat of the song, often pretending the decoration is alive.
why_now: The song is synonymous with 'spooky season' and is trending for comedic prop-based content.
brand_use: A retail brand can 'animate' their products or mannequins to the beat, giving them a 'haunted' but fun personality.
example_brief: A home goods store shows a toaster 'dancing' to the beat of Goo Goo Muck.

name: The Process (BTS)
what: A step-by-step reveal of the tools, materials, and effort that goes into creating a product or service.
why_now: Transparency and 'craft' content are currently outperforming polished ads.
brand_use: An agency can show the 'process' of a photoshoot—from moodboard to final edit—to demonstrate expertise and value.
example_brief: A jewelry brand shows the raw gold being melted down before cutting to the final polished ring.

name: Oops, wrong way
what: Creators start with a text overlay about a random opinion, then 'accidentally' flip the camera to show how that opinion actually benefits them.
why_now: It’s a clever way to show brand benefits without being 'preachy.'
brand_use: A brand can use this to show a 'hack.' Text: 'I hate when people find out about this secret sale,' then flip the camera to show the creator filling their cart.
example_brief: A skincare brand: 'I hate when people have clear skin,' flips to show the creator using the brand's new cleanser.
